div.head: Hn Lond 4
div.ab: Et infra muros ciuitatis nullus hospitetur, neque de mea familia neque de alia ui alicui hospitium liberetur.
Et infra muros civitatis nullus hospitetur, neque de mea familia neque de alia vi alicui [hospitium] liberatur.
And no-one shall be billeted within the walls of the city nor shall hospitality be forcibly exacted for anyone belonging to my household or to any other.
div.note: Added October 2026 from Robertson pp. 288–289 (text and translation); Liebermann’s text added from Gesetze I p. 525, October 2026 (two independent readings of the page images)

omitted in Cc Cust; written above Horn

Vgl. Gl Gastung 3a; über die Einquartierung in London durch den königlichen Marschall s. Round King's serjeants 88.—Für die Lesart vi sprechen auch die Freibriefe für Colchester (wo erstes neque fehlt), Edinburgh; Ballard 87. [Heinrich IV. privilegierte 1081 Lucca: ut nostrum regale palatium intra civitatem . . non edificent, aut inibi vi hospitia capiantur; Stumpf Kaiserurkunden n. 2833]

Cf. Gl Gastung 3a; on billeting in London by the royal marshal see Round King's serjeants 88.—The reading vi is also supported by the charters for Colchester (where the first neque is missing) and Edinburgh; Ballard 87. [In 1081 Henry IV granted Lucca the privilege ut nostrum regale palatium intra civitatem . . non edificent, aut inibi vi hospitia capiantur; Stumpf Kaiserurkunden n. 2833]

Die Lesart nisi, auch von Round angenommen, erklärt Stubbs (Lect. 125): ‘unless the duty of entertaining him be assigned to some particular person to secure the safety and responsibility of the stranger entertained’—offenbar eine Künstelei, die man nicht hinter diesem einfachen Stile wittern darf. Vielleicht verstanden die nisi bevorzugenden Abschreiber eher ungenau liberare entweder als ‘freiwillig liefern’ oder als ‘bezahlen’. In Rouen steht zwar nisi per proprium marescallum civitatis; ein solches dem Sinne des redenden Königs fremdes, ja entgegengesetztes, Subjekt konnte aber wohl ein Londoner sich nicht als elliptisch zu liberare hinzudenken; Giry Établ. de Rouen II 63

The reading nisi, which Round also accepts, is explained by Stubbs (Lect. 125): ‘unless the duty of entertaining him be assigned to some particular person to secure the safety and responsibility of the stranger entertained’—obviously an artificiality that one should not suspect behind this simple style. Perhaps the copyists who preferred nisi understood liberare, rather inexactly, either as ‘to supply voluntarily’ or as ‘to pay’. At Rouen, it is true, the text reads nisi per proprium marescallum civitatis; but a Londoner could probably not have supplied in thought such a subject, foreign to, indeed contrary to, the meaning of the king who is speaking, as understood elliptically with liberare; Giry Établ. de Rouen II 63
